subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-12, as we all know, caps post-secondary educational transfers at six and five rather than allowing the normal increase to take place. One of the most serious things about the Bill, indicating how clearly the Government derogates from the authority of Parliament, is that it is retroactive for a full year. Some $118 million has already been taken out of post-secondary educational transfers in the fiscal year just ended; we are now passing the Bill to authorize that capping. We tried our best, of course, to pass an amendment which would have required the restoration of the $118 million. Unfortunately, we were not able to get that amendment through.
I would also like to point out the seriousness of this Bill in that in other areas, for example, medicare, the federal Government has not applied six and five to its transfers to the provinces, only in post-secondary education. The Government intends to continue an even more serious withdrawal of funds in 1984-85.
It is rather odd, too, that the federal Government says that the six and five capping is going to cease, I believe in June, just at the very moment it is no longer going to be part of the federal Government's policy to enforce six and five in the public sector. It is saying, however, that for last year and for the whole of the fiscal year we are now beginning, we will continue limiting our post-secondary educational transfers to the provinces. It seems to me that it is very difficult, therefore, for the Government to have any credibility at all when it says, as it does, and as the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) said only yesterday, that it is concerned about the future of post-secondary education in this country.
One of the difficulties with the way we presently fund post-secondary education is that there is no accountability. Whether the money is in tax points or equalized transfers, there is no way the Parliament of Canada, representing the

April 5, 1984
Established Programs Financing
taxpayers, can know how that money is going to be spent. It is not earmarked. The provinces can spend that money any way they please. Some of them indeed have been doing so and have not been directing these moneys intended for post-secondary education to post-secondary education. Ever since block funding was started in 1977, we in this Party have argued that it was a mistake and was financially irresponsible.
Yesterday we argued, through an amendment to this Bill which was debated in the House, that there should be accountability, at least for the portion of the funding for post-secondary education that is derived from the increase in federal transfers, the six and five that this Bill authorizes. We should be able to direct the money to be spent for the purposes intended. By that amendment yesterday we were striving for fiscal accountability. Yet when we voted on that amendment, neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives supported it. I am especially puzzled that the Conservatives did not support it. They have argued time and again for fiscal accountability and responsibility with the taxpayers' money. It is the federal taxpayers' money which is going to the provinces for postsecondary educational funding. Surely if we have any sense of responsibility and accountability in the system we should have a requirement, as we could and as we did before 1977, that money allocated for post-secondary education should be spent on post-secondary education.
The amendment yesterday would have been a clear signal to everyone that those provinces which have not been spending money for the purposes intended should be doing so. Had the other two Parties voted for the amendment, it would have been a clear signal to the people of the country that we represent the taxpayers of Canada in a responsible fashion. It would have been a clear signal that the federal Government of Canada cares about the future of post-secondary education on behalf of all Canadians. Perhaps a speaker from the Conservative Party will explain to us all why they voted against fiscal accountability. I do not expect anyone from the Liberal Party to try to explain it because they did not even put up a speaker to introduce third reading of this Bill.
In debating Bill C-12, this Party particularly has been trying to bring to the attention of the House and the Government the real crisis in our post-secondary educational institutions. The institutions themselves, the students who attend them and the faculties which teach and do research in them are experiencing crises of major dimensions. In the United States they have been restraining and cutting back with regard to Government services. They have not been cutting back on education. Indeed, they have been dramatically increasing their expenditures on post-secondary education at the federal level. They know that if they are going to have and sustain an economic recovery in the United States, there must be an educated society to sustain it. They know, as we should know, that we have already moved into the post-industrial society and into the information-based society. The prime criterion of survival, let alone of flourishing in such a society, is knowledgeable and informed people. While manual skills are still
important, mental skills are, more than in any other society, absolutely vital to the survival of a post-industrial way of life.
Indeed, Canada has taken the lead in the past, but rather than follow this example of taking the lead in recognizing what are the needs of the future, it is continuing to underfund seriously its post-secondary educational institutions. It is making it impossible for this society to respond adequately to a changing economic climate. The Government is putting a cap on post-secondary educational spending at the very moment when the United States, our closest neighbour, is substantially and, some would say, dramatically increasing its spending on post-secondary educational institutions.
There are innumerable horror stories being told now about what is happening in our post-secondary educational institutions. Just last week, the President of the University of British Columbia, George Pederson, declared that the university is in a state of financial exigency, in the legal sense of that word, which means that people will have to be laid off, both faculty and staff, and many programs dismantled.
Just a few days ago there was a story that headhunters are already raiding a faculty that has taken years to build up. The commerce and business faculty is one of the most vulnerable at UBC because it has such an excellent reputation, as has been noted by the Wall Street Journal and by many educational institutions across the country and in the United States. The Dean of Business and Commerce, Peter Lusztig, says that the place could be cleaned out in 10 or 12 months. This is not just idle talk, this is what is foreseen within 10 or 12 months.
1 recently reviewed what is happening at Cariboo College in Kamloops. The college has cut its continuing educational program, which has effectively disenfranchised some 6,000 students. Three satellite campuses of Cariboo College, which were previously funded directly by the provincial Government, are now required to obtain their funding from their college operating grants which, in turn, are being capped or substantially reduced as a result of federal Government action. It is likely that these satellite campuses will be forced to close, making rural accessibility an even greater problem than it is now.
In an effort to generate funds, Cariboo College is launching a program to recruit groups of 20 students from Hong Kong to travel to Kamloops for eight months at a cost of $7,500 per student in order to take a type of correspondence course at the college. There is even talk among the college's board members about building a hotel next to the college to accommodate the students. Is this what post-secondary education in Canada is all about? Is it about making a profit from foreign students while denying education to Canadian students who cannot afford the unreasonable costs?
The costs are becoming unreasonable. In my province, the Government has decided that no more grants will be given to students. There will be no grants whatsoever. I agree that other provinces, with one exception, have not gone that far. But the Province of British Columbia has decided that only
April 5, 1984

loans will be available from now on. There will be no grants for those in financial need, only loans.
Last year a student at Douglas College in my riding had received a $1,000 loan and a $1,000 grant. This year his loan has to be $2,000 because his grant is only $90. He can look forward next year, if he is still able to attend the college, to receiving no grant at all. He says he will probably not be able to continue at University when he must operate solely on loans which increase every year.
1 was talking to another person at Douglas College who has been declared ineligible even for a loan. The lady is in her thirties. She is a single mother, recently separated from her husband. In the separation agreement she was allowed the car. Because she was allowed the car, she has been denied the loan and she has ended up on welfare. I give these examples and there are thousands more one can give. The underfunding of research in our communities is another area we can talk about, and some of our members will be talking about it in the course of this third reading debate.
We are arriving at a situation at which our colleges and universities will become second-class institutions, at which they will no longer be able to do the kind of research they have done in the past. An example of that is the university from which I graduated, Queen's University, which used to be among the top ten in North America in terms of the quality of its library. A library is one of the most important things a university has, but the Queen's University library is now, I think, ranked 87th, right in there with the University of Connecticut.
1 wonder whether Members of the House realize what a crisis we are in. I wonder whether Members of the Cabinet realize what a crisis we are in. The Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), who is not here today but who is generally available when we discuss in committee matters concerning post-secondary education, apparently has no clout in Cabinet whatsoever. One of the reasons for that is that he has not yet got a handle on the problems facing our institutions. He does not know, for example, where the $118 million went that should have gone to post-secondary education funding in 1983-84. I asked him about this in committee, as some Hon. Members here will recall. He did not know. He threw out all kinds of ideas about where that $118 million might have gone, because it has been spent, it was not saved. It was spent in 1983-84. He threw out a variety of ideas about where it might have gone, and then said the bulk of it went into the Canada Student Loans Program. He did not even know that that is a loan program, and not a grant program. I wish it were a grant program. But he talked as if it were a grant program, and said that that is where a lot of the $118 million had gone. That is ridiculous. He did not know, although he announced the creation of a task force to look into post-secondary educational funding. He announced that A1 Johnson, a very excellent choice in my view, would be heading the task force. He announced that in committee, but when I asked who were the members of the
Established Programs Financing task force, he did not know. When 1 asked for the terms of reference of the task force, he could not provide them. When I telephoned just yesterday to get the terms of reference, they were still not available.
How can a Minister who does not know where the $118 million went-and it should have gone to the provinces for post-secondary educational funding-have very much influence? How can a Minister, who sets up a task force without being able to say what are its terms of reference, have very much influence with other Ministers in the Cabinet of Canada?
We have been inundated with telegrams and letters from the post-secondary educational sector. In the last few days I have received letters and telegrams from the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Students, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, and from many other groups. In its telegram, the Canadian Federation of Students expressed its continuing opposition to the passage of Bill C-12. It reads:
This Bill will result in the loss of $378 million over a two-year period. GFS urges that the six and five limitation clause be eliminated, that funds for education ... be earmarked, and that a national dialogue on the funding and direction of post-secondary education in Canada commence immediately.
The Canadian Association of University Teachers, in its telegram to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLar-en), who undoubtedly has not read it, wrote:
The Canadian Association of University Teachers deplores federal Government's action restricting funds for post-secondary education through Bill C-12. All Canadian governments should be increasing, not decreasing, accessibility to higher education so that young people of our country may receive education that will equip them for life in the remaining decades of this century and in the 21st century. CAUT calls upon the federal Government to reconsider its position, particularly since it has decided to restrict only the area of post-secondary education among the transfer programs to the provinces.
A letter from the Executive Director of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada pointed out that transfers for post-secondary education have been singled out for application of the six and five program at the very moment when enrolment demands have continued to increase. In his letter, Dr. Gillmore wrote:
Universities desperately need additional support to maintain standards of excellence and to respond to increasing needs of a broad spectrum of Canadian society.
The continued imposition of six and five on higher education as proposed in Bill C-12 will not serve the best interests of the country at this time.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, unfortunately the Conservative Party supported the six and fiving as a general principle in the original legislation. Perhaps, if it had not supported that general principle, we would not be fighting this battle today for the removal of the six and five limitation on post-secondary educational transfers. In more recent days its Members have realized the crisis of the universities and colleges in our society. I repeat, it is a crisis of the institutions themselves, of the potential research which can and should be done in those institutions, of the teaching programs which should be made available to our young people and, perhaps

April 5, 1984
Established Programs Financing
above all, a crisis for our society that we will not be able to bring young people and older people into the post-secondary educational stream.
It is a complete denial of what the Government did in the post-World War II period for veterans. It was one of the most outstanding programs a Canadian government has ever implemented. What the Government is doing now is a complete denial of that. That was a program of making postsecondary education accessible to every veteran who wanted it. They did not keep jacking up entrance standards. They said everyone who was qualified-50 per cent in those days-could attend university or college. They came in flocks and enriched society; indeed they made post-war society what it was. Now the Government turns its back on the principle then established.
The Governments of many of the provinces turned their backs as well on the principle of accessibility to higher education. Ontario and British Columbia are perhaps the two most serious cases in point. Both are Tory governments. One is called a Socred government, but it is a Tory government. In less than a year in my province we will see this crisis in our post-secondary educational institutions so deepened that it may be too late to get out of it. Surely the federal Government and Parliament, by withdrawing this Bill and by allowing the natural increase, which is still a very modest increase, in postsecondary educational funding to take place, could show that they understand the nature of the crisis in post-secondary education, that they are not prepared to wait until tomorrow to do something about the crisis and that they are prepared to act now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member who just spoke. She referred to decreasing enrolments and possible cutbacks in enrolments. I have a clipping from the Sunday Star of February 12, 1984, in which the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) was reported as speaking at a conference in Victoria. She said:
-a study of national educational standards is needed, in consultation with the provinces and industry.
The article continued:
She said that, if such a review found there were too many university applicants, then perhaps entrance standards should be raised.
"I don't think there is a birthright to complete a university degree if you're a mediocre student.
"I have the feeling that you should reserve university, especially the way our funding is structured-"
Also the Minister said that she favoured a European model that stresses academic competence. The article continued:
"In order to enter university there, you have to go through a competition and be the best."
Could the Hon. Member give her comments on this story, especially on what she feels this kind of restricted entrance and the raising of entrance requirements would do to students who came from small towns and rural areas, as well as young people from some of the cultural minorities?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) does not know what the situation is in Europe. Indeed, there has been a greater degree of accessibility for students in lower income groups than we have seen in this country. The Minister of State for Youth apparently is not aware of the program for veterans that I was speaking of earlier. In those days you did not need to have some terrifically high marks in order to get into university. On the contrary, everyone was encouraged to go. If they could not make it, somewhere along the line they would stop and do something else with their lives, but everyone was given the opportunity. The Government has gone back on that principle.
There is no question in my mind that if you restrict university and college only to students who have a very high grade, you are restricting a very large number of students, many from communities that have not had opportunities in high school or in their home background to develop the kinds of skills that are required to get those very high grades. You are restricting entrance on a class basis the minute you pursue the course of action that the Minister of State for Youth is suggesting.
In my view that is not the course of action Canadians want to see followed. Nor has it been the actual course of action that most Canadian Governments have followed until the past two years. What we are trying to do and trying to persuade the Minister of State for Youth, if she is going to continue in that portfolio for any length of time, is to understand that Canadians do not want a return to the really old days, which is what she apparently wants, of an educational system for the elite only.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) referred to the cuts in universities. I would like her to be more specific. I understand, for example, that there is a projection that the budget of UBC may be cut a total of about 24 per cent over the next four years, beginning now. It is suggested that that will be made up largely by an increase in student fees. Does the Hon. Member have any information as to how that may reduce the student enrolment, whether it will be possible to make up that 24 per cent through student fees if the students simply do not come, and whether there is a danger that functions of the university that are very important to the culture and economy of British Columbia may simply have to be closed?

Mr. Speaker, there is already at UBC a cutback in the number of students that they will take in the fall of this year. Many, many qualified students will be denied the right to come to the university, many more because fees are being raised by 33W per cent. The Government has now taken away
April 5, 1984

all of the grant system and is only providing loans. Many will not be able to come because of that.
Likely the increase in fees and the smaller number of students will not be of all that much help in reducing the enormous deficit faced by the University of British Columbia. Probably it will not help that much. That is why the university is saying that it will have to cut back drastically on programs. That is why head-hunters are already on the campus trying to pick up the good faculty members and persuade them to go elsewhere in the country. In other words, the excellence of the university is very seriously threatened. The university will not be able to keep its best programs and faculty. It is going to be a vicious circle. There will be fewer students because the students cannot afford to go. There will be higher and higher tuition fees which students will not be able to pay. That will cut back on the number of students attending. In order to make up this incredible deficit, they will have to cut programs.
That is why the president of that university-its position is not dissimilar from that of other universities in the province by the way-has been speaking so forcibly against Bills such as we are now debating.

speechtext:
It is shameful and unbelievable how a Government that claims to be committed to higher education, to bringing this country into the 20th century, to attempting to achieve 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product through research and development, a Government that claims to be enlightened, brings in measures that knocks the support away from one of our major institutions, our universities.
By knocking away the support that has been diligently built up over the years in terms of the funding of our university system, with this and previous Bills that have been introduced, especially by the present Government, it is destroying our universities in Canada. This is being done at a time when our young people are in desperate straits. Statistics show that one of every five is unemployed; some 20 per cent of our young people are unemployed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has said that this is a marvellous thing because it shows that four or five young people are able to find some form of employment. He is willing to write off 20 per cent of this generation. Even though some have been able to find some
Established Programs Financing form of employment, many are not able to find meaningful employment.
At the same time that this is occurring, the doors to our universities are slowly creaking shut on them. Normally, when there has been high unemployment among young people, they tend to go to university to better their education in order to be in a better position to get a job, a career, and to live their lives. This opportunity is now being shut off.
It is amazing to those of us in this part of the House who see how the Government continues with Bill C-12. Surely the Government has heard from the university community, the students and administrators. When I was in committee, we heard of the drastic effects this will have on the universities and the opportunities for young Canadians to acquire a decent education to enable them to be competitive in the 20th century. It is having a drastic effect.
I am the critic for my Party in the area of science and technology. In terms of the natural sciences, we know that the equipment at the universities is in a deplorable state. Very often the computers in high schools are of better quality and are more up to date than those in the universities where the equipment is outdated. Students who graduate and go into the private market are not capable of dealing with the new and better equipment that they find, so they have to be retrained. Because the universities lack the finances to get the up to date equipment, the graduates are not capable of dealing with the equipment that is in the workplace. This is one example of the inadequacy and underfunding of our university system.
As well, we see that the natural sciences have been lucky in some ways that their funding has kept pace with the real increase in the cost to universities. The inflation rate for books and scientific equipment is much higher than the general inflationary increase. The increase in funding to organizations like NSERC has kept pace with the real increased costs of scientific equipment and books. The social sciences have suffered, however. The Government has totally ignored them and has cut back very significantly on the granting of funds to the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. They have a deplorable background.
We have cuts in payments to universities at both the provincial and federal level. We have increased unemployment among young people and, therefore, an increased demand for university places and further cuts for the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. That is one of the areas of major funding for university people in the social sciences and in the humanities.
There are three different attacks on young people in the university system. In continues to amaze us how the Government, in its ignorance, can continue with these attacks. Is it not concerned with the future? Is it not concerned that these young people have the education to get meaningful employment in the 20th century? It is something that I cannot understand.

April 5, 1984
Established Programs Financing
Let me go back to the question of research and development, Mr. Speaker. A recent report on technologies in Ontario was dealt with in an article in the Globe and Mail on Tuesday, April 3, 1984, and states as follows:
"Canadian managers have tended to be older and less educated than their counterparts in the United States and this has been suggested as a reason for the poor rates of technology diffusion in Canada," says the budget paper.
It goes on to say:
The budget paper notes that in 1980 41.4 per cent of Ontario's 20- to 24-year olds were attending post-secondary institutions while 57.1 per cent of Americans in the same age group were attending colleges or universities.
That is a dismal record for Canada. It is no wonder we are lagging behind in research and development in this country. It is no wonder we are having great difficulty achieving the Governments' objective of allocating 1.5 per cent of the Gross National Product to research and development. One of the reasons for our difficulties is that we do not have the trained manpower to enable us to reach that goal. And we do not have the trained manpower because the universities are not in a position to produce trained manpower. Do the Government thinkers and planners not realize the simple fact that they cannot, like King Canute, demand that the tides flow back or demand that all at once we have trained personnel to enable us to reach our national goal in research and development? Do they not know that these things must be planned for and that there must be institutions that would allow people to be trained so that they can reach that goal? Am I missing something here, Mr. Speaker? Do the government planners not recognize this fact? It seems that they do not.
The Government is proudly touting the centres of excellence it is developing. In fact, it is hoping that some of our researchers in the social sciences and humanities and the natural sciences will be able to find employment in these centres of excellence. I have no objection to the funding and the efforts that have gone into creating centres of excellence, but surely not at the expense of the centres of excellence we already have-our universities.
What is the sense of destroying our universities in order to build something else? If we are to have centres of excellence in new areas, then I think all Canadians would welcome that, but surely not at the expense of the centres of excellence we already have. Canadian universities are internationally known. They have produced outstanding graduates in all fields, but our ability to do that in the future has been seriously hampered by the efforts of the Government.
Just to reiterate and strengthen the claim of the universities and the role they play, I should like to place on the record a comment by Dr. George Keyworth, the science adviser to the President of the United States who said:
-no other research institutions give as much return on investment as universities in the long term-not federal labs, nor non-profit organizations, not industry. No other institutions produce both knowledge and people.
I am afraid our mad hatters on the other side of the aisle have no recognition of that basic fact and no appreciation of the contributions the universities have made.
The federal Government claims that it is not responsible for the bad state the universities are in; it blames the provinces, and the provinces of course blame the federal Government. The two are blaming each other, and in the meantime our universities are going down the tube because neither of them is willing to take responsibility for this deplorable state. That is just not good enough. Obviously both levels of Government are to blame; obviously the funding arrangement does not ensure that federal moneys going to higher education are in fact spent on higher education. That is something that this Party deplored when block funding was introduced in the seventies, and we continue to deplore it.
What is needed is a national co-operative effort to ensure that our universities do not go down the drain. That means co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces. It must be recognized that the provinces have a historic responsibility to education and higher education and, on the other hand, it must also be recognized that there is a national interest in maintaining a university system across the country which will allow mobility of knowledge and of students and will ensure a high degree of technical, social and humanistic excellence. There are both federal and provincial interests, but we are finding that those interests are being used as an excuse to avoid responsibility for the deplorable situation.
I am afraid our universities are falling between the slats, so to speak. They are suffering, young Canadians are suffering, and Canada as a whole will suffer as we enter the 20th century.
1 sat in committee and listened to the students present their brief. They rightly pointed out that the federal Government is not entirely innocent in the matter of the decrease of university funding by the provinces. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I will quote directly from their brief. It reads:
Unfortunately, this Bill does nothing to ensure that even the limited funds will be used for the purpose for which they are being allotted.
And they mean federal funds going toward higher education. The brief continues:
Moreover, it is somewhat hypocritical of the federal Government to scapegoat the provinces, when limiting provincial spending was part of the original strategy behind the 1976 EPF negotiations. Prime Minister Trudeau stated at the time, that the 1976 fiscal arrangements proposal-
And the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is quoted as saying:
-suits the current and future imperative, namely fiscal restraint, in that the provinces will have a greater incentive to implement what are admittedly difficult measures designed to restrain spending in these fields.

It was so obvious, Mr. Speaker, how the two Parties came together to vote down that amendment, because the Official Opposition was acting in the interests of the provincial Tory Governments which are not interested in accountability, and the federal Government was acting in its own self-interest because it has been using provincial cutbacks as an excuse to make their own cuts. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker referred in his remarks to the necessity of having a large number of educated people to continue, among other things, the technological development and expansion of Canada. He also referred to the centres of excellence in the Government's proposals. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on whether he thinks the new or untried centres of excellence will be able to do better because they are more flexible, or will they do worse because they have no background in developing the new kinds of technology which this country needs? subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is an excellent question, Mr. Speaker. Many of us are trying to understand what the Government is attempting to do with its centres of excellence. On the surface they sound like good ideas. You bring together trained and specialized people and focus on the specific subject area. However, as I quoted, the scientific adviser to the President of the United States said that federal Government, private and non-profit labs, are no substitute for excellence as far as university labs are concerned. These centres of excellence should not replace the existing ones, our universities.
Another concern I have is whether the federal Government is attempting to mould higher education and learning in this country so that only those projects politically more interesting or rewarding get funding, whereas the mundane administration, the brick and mortar of universities, the buildings and so on, receive less and less funding. This was expressed by the Canadian association of University Teachers in December of last year in its brief to the Royal Commission on the Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada. What I am concerned about, Mr. Speaker, is that the centres of excellence are really picking up certain parts of science and technology for development, and leaving all sorts of other areas aside. That would distort research and development in Canada which would be a great detriment to our society.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned a certain amendment put forward by the NDP. We of course voted against that amendment because it made absolutely no sense. There was really no point in demanding an accounting of the federal cash contributions to the provincial Governments because those amounts are far less than what is actually spent in every province. What is the point in putting the bureaucracy to that wasted time and effort?
You will recall, Sir, that a very proper amendment was put forward by the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) and moved in this House by the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). It was accepted by all sides of the House. That amendment represents probably the only worth-while thing in the Bill at all. It required the following:
(3) Beginning in the 1983-84 fiscal year the Minister shall report annually to Parliament on:
(a)	cash transfers to each province for post-secondary education under Established Programs Financing;
(b)	expenditures by each province on post-secondary education;
(c)	to the extent appropriate, other programs of federal support to or involvement in post-secondary education;
(d)	the effectiveness of these federal expenditures and programs in moving towards Canada's educational and economic goals; and
(e)	the results of any consultations with the Council of Ministers of Education of Canada-
That makes a lot of sense, Mr. Speaker.
I want to talk about the positive things in this Bill before I tell you why this Party cannot accept the Bill in its form and intent. This amendment for the first time gives Members of Parliament an accounting of the cash and tax transfers allotted to post-secondary education. When we have an accounting of the money the federal Government spends through its manpower programs, assistance to training and education and research and development at universities, we can properly determine whether the block funding arrangement we presently have in the established programs financing system is working.
April 5, 1984

Accusations go back and forth, Sir. The provinces accuse the federal Government of not carrying its weight. The federal Government says that the provinces get tax transfers and use the money to build roads, bridges and to look after welfare, but do not use it where it should be used, that is, for postsecondary education. Well, Sir, we will find out in the reports made to this House every year. The first report is for the fiscal year beginning April 1. Therefore, in 1986 we will get the report for the 1984-85 year on what has been spent.
That brings me to the basic principles of this Party in dealing with education and training. We have said that there are four basic pillars on which we would form the Government of this country and attempt to rebuild the economy. The first principle, of course, is one that we have been dealing with through the month of March, the methods that must be used to reduce interest rates and improve the credit worthiness of businesses. The other three pillars are technology, training and trade. Concerning technology and training, the transfers to post-secondary education are vital. We are living in an age when the hewers of wood and drawers of water are not going to have jobs. Just look at this morning's paper, Sir, and you will see that one in five persons in British Columbia lives on welfare or unemployment insurance. Why?

speechtext: Good Tory Government in B.C.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Because the economy of that province is closely tied to natural resource exports and those resources are not hot on the world market today. The figures from British Columbia are disastrous. The newspaper article compares them with those for the Province of Ontario. That province has a population close to four times as large as that of B.C., and its unemployment and welfare problems are considerably smaller. The answer is this: we must have a society which exports not just coal, lumber and copper. We must have a society that exports high technology, the manufactured goods which make the world turn around better. We can only do this if we as a nation are prepared to invest in higher technology and more technology. It may be the robotics in the factories; it may be new methods of processing raw materials; it may be new methods of transporting goods. However, it must be in the high technology field so that we can be productive enough, and therefore competitive enough, to keep our people working and have the kind of life which we want and expect to have. We will not do that if we cut back on transfers to post-secondary education.
This Bill cuts back on cash transfers. It cuts back on the money imputed to come from other transfers as well. It cuts back $118 million in the past fiscal year. It cuts back a further $260 million in the fiscal year just starting, for a total cutback of $378 million. 1 would like to read into the record the types of things that are happening.
If this Bill is passed, the cash which my Province of Ontario will receive will be reduced by $41.7 million in 1983-84 and by a further $92 million in 1984-85, for a total reduction of
Established Programs Financing $133.7 million. That is going to come out of the money available to train young people. That is going to come out of the money available to do something about the problems at Queen's University, the University of Toronto, the University of Western Ontario and the other universities in Ontario. That is going to make the enrolment crunch even worse. Young people coming out of Grade 13 in Ontario must have at least an 80 per cent average to get into some courses in some of the universities. Our young people do not just have to be competent; they have to be exceptionally brilliant, highly trained and highly successful in getting the required marks. That is going to be very, very hard on them. All sorts of aggressive young people will not have the opportunity of furthering their education.
Yesterday I spent some time at the University of Western Ontario. I did some work on tax simplification with the graduate students of the business school there. In the morning I was in my constituency office and had two young people visit me there. They wanted to take a course at Sheridon College in connection with computer programming. The Government was going to help finance that course, but because of bureaucratic red tape these young people will perhaps not be able to get into the course. They have been waiting for six months doing temporary part-time work while waiting to get into this course. Many courses are not available because $41 million is being taken out of the Province of Ontario this year and an additional $90 million next year.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) can say that these cutbacks come as a result of the six and five program and are part of reducing inflation. Reducing the transfers from one government's spending ability to another government's spending ability does not reduce inflation. If that $118 million had been left in the hands of the taxpayers of Canada, that may have helped them. It was taken anyway. The only result is that the money is not transferred to the provincial government, therefore the federal Government has money to spend on other more apparent, but not necessarily more important, programs. Sir, that money should not be spent in other fields. That money should have been transferred to the provinces. The Government should follow through on the amendment to this Bill and make sure that the money goes where it is supposed to go, to building and maintaining libraries and laboratories. It should go to making sure that classrooms have competent instructors and professors.
This Bill is a bad Bill. It hurts Canada. I call as my witness to that a candidate for the leadership of the Liberal Party, the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). I quote from the Montreal Gazette as follows:
During his speech and talking to reporters later, Roberts said there is a crisis in post-secondary education and there must be stronger federal participation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) a question for clarification. Did I understand him to say that the Party on whose behalf he is speaking, the Conservative Party, is in favour of a system whereby we in this Parliament can be guaranteed that the moneys transferred to the provinces for post-secondary education will in fact be spent by the provinces on post-secondary education?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the big advantages of the amendment that was moved and passed yesterday is that it is an amendment of disclosure. While amendments of disclosure do not guarantee anything, they can become exceptionally embarrassing for those who do not spend what they receive. Therefore, they tend to force a national policy on education.
Obviously this Parliament has no direct ability to deal with the problems of education. While it may be argued that we can talk about manpower training or that the economic powers of the country involve training, which they certainly do, it is quite clear in terms of the institutional spending of money in educational facilities that, according to our Canada Act, we do not have that power.
When money is being paid from the federal Treasury to the provinces and the disclosure provisions in this statute make it clear that the provinces are not doing their share and are using the money for something other than post-secondary education, then it would behoove us as Members of Parliament to say that the transfers will have to be reduced and we will have to find another way of solving the problem.
I suggest to the Hon. Member that the great advantage of this amendment is that it gives us, for the first time, an idea of where the money is going, on what it is being spent, and whether it is being spent on its intended use.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, of course, all Parties have agreed to this amendment to which the Hon. Member has just referred at the meeting of the task force on fiscal federalism in 1981. As the Hon. Member said, it is an amendment requiring disclosure.
I gather that what he is saying is that his Party will not take any action now to ensure that the provinces are spending federal moneys for which the moneys were designed. It seems to me that he is denying the authority of the federal Parliament to ensure that the federal taxpayers' money that is going to the provinces is spent for its intended purpose. He is going
April 5, 1984

to wait until after the first year when the disclosure amendment that was passed yesterday becomes effective. This brings me to my second question.
The Elon. Member knows that if we do enough digging, which I and I am sure he has done, we can get a picture now of what the different provinces are doing with the tax points and cash transfers that they receive. Indeed, we have done enough digging to know that his province and mine have not kept up their share of the spending on post-secondary education to anything like what it was in the pre 1977 period.
That being the case, why does he say that his Party will just wait until the amendment that was passed yesterday takes effect? That will be a long time from now. Would he not wish to put the position of his Party on the whole question of accountability on the record now?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member suggests that we know what the provinces are doing. Well, we do not know. We know what the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), through his officials, thinks they are doing. However, the question of what in fact they are doing depends, to a large extent, on the interpretation of what is properly post-secondary education.
Let me give an example. In the Province of Ontario the secondary school system is designed to go to Grade 13. That is one year longer than in other provinces. The question is whether the work, even in Grade 12 in Ontario, is not partially post-secondary.
In the Province of Quebec we see the CEGEP system, and in Newfoundland there are some instances when young people attend university after Grade 11. There are varying opinions as to what is post-secondary education, which makes it difficult to determine from province to province, without some real input and agreed method of determination, whether the provinces are in fact spending what they should spend.
Furthermore, there was a question about whether the transfer, which was a total transfer until the introduction of this Bill, was properly divided at roughly 33 per cent and 67 per cent. In its appropriations, the Government has always said that the transfer for post-secondary education is 32.1 per cent, I believe, of the total EPF transfer, and the balance is for medical care. However, that position has not generally been accepted by the provinces.
If one accepts that it is 32 per cent of the transfer, we may find that some of the provinces are only spending 35 per cent or 40 per cent of the education money, with the balance coming in tax transfers and cash from the federal government. The problem has been that until this Bill, it has not been determined that legislatively that is the correct percentage in the transfer system. Until the passage of this Bill, the provinces could easily say, "Well, it is a block fund. We are using the block fund for medicare concerns, for hospital concerns, for this and that concern, and, of course, for post-secondary education". One of the other advantages of this Bill is that at least it divides the fund and it divides it legislatively.

Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) state that the federal Government has been cutting back in the amount of funding for post-secondary school education. I think I should draw to his attention the fact that the federal contribution back in 1974-75 amounted to 49.19 per cent and the provincial contribution was 31.12 per cent. Yet by 1981-82 the federal contribution rose to 56.89 per cent and the provincial contribution declined to 21 per cent.
I would further like to point out to the Hon. Member that at the present time in Ontario the Government of Canada provides over 56 per cent and the province 21 per cent, and other contributions, such as for tuition, amount to 21.80 per cent. I suggest that his statement that the federal Government is cutting back is not factual. In fact, the federal Government has increased its share over the years. It has been the provincial government of Ontario that has been cutting back.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that, after the debate over this past several weeks in and out of the House and in and out of committee, we still have to face the Government's determination to cut $378 million from the funding for post-secondary institutions in Canada over the next two years. It is becoming typical of this Government to be carrying it out in an arrogant way, a way that would be illegal for any other body, namely, to make the cuts retroactive. Of course, a government that can rule that Tuesday is Monday can rule that 1984 is 1983 when it wants to. 1 am mainly sorry because it is a very untimely block and constriction on Canada's development.
A previous speaker has referred to the arrangement at the end of World War II when many of us coming out of the forces benefited from the program of the Department of Veterans Affairs. We were very grateful for it. 1 want to make

April 5, 1984
Established Programs Financing
the comparison. What that program did in part, and perhaps the most important part of it, was to enable a whole section of Canadians to attend university who otherwise would never have been able to do so, although some of us would have. Some of us came from families with the financial means to assist us and others of us had been sufficiently trained to enable us to compete for scholarships and things like that. But many did not have that advantage. Many who had the same native intelligence as we did, or perhaps more, and many who had just as much motivation and just as much self-discipline as we did would not have got to university. For example, during the 1930s people did not get there. I knew some who did not get there. But because the Government, even though it was a Liberal Government at that time, chose to give generous support and allowances to the students, we have a whole generation of people who have been a vital part of the development of Canada during the past 40 years.
It is very sad that this Government, although not alone but it has been leading, has decided to turn its back on that sort of ideal. Of course, the DVA funding is long past. There have been ups and downs in the rate at which governments would lend or grant allowances to students. At no time was there any suggestion that these grants or loans were just a form of babysitting, teen sitting, or welfare. They were based on performance. A student had to be able to achieve a certain agreed level if he was to continue receiving those grants and loans. But now those grants and loans are being seriously cut back right across the country. They are being cut back not only because of the federal Government's policy but, as I say, with the federal Government leading.
The Hon. Member across the way would like to use percentages to pretend there has not been a cut, but in fact, as everybody who looks at figures knows, there has been a cut. I agree with the Hon. Member from Mississauga that the reduction is in the range of over $41 million in the past year and $92 million in the coming year for the Province of Ontario. I also agree with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) that this will have a very bad effect on Canada. He claims it will make us hewers of water and drawers of wood. I am not quite sure what that means, but 1 am familiar with the danger of being hewers of wood and drawers of water. Perhaps he has not come out of the ice age and thinks we will have to hew ice. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I agree with him that there is a bleak future for Ontario and for the rest of Canada when we cut back on education funding in the age which has been called the age of the information revolution. The number of students in Ontario will be reduced through the action of that province primarily.
They make excuses that it is this federal cut, but the Ontario Government has taken its own cuts as well. It will be reducing the grants, raising the fees, or forcing universities to raise fees and, as a result, the number of students will be reduced. Access to universities will be restricted, but not to the intellectual elite and not to those with high marks. Although that is being talked about, and there is some gesture in that direction, that would be too harsh an action to take. Primarily
access to university will be given to students whose parents have money.
The Government of Ontario will also alter fundamentally the structures of Ontario universities through what it calls a program of specialization. Universities will be told to close departments. If a person wants to study a certain discipline, perhaps he will have to leave the city in which he resides with his parents. Instead of travelling by foot, by bicycle or by public transit to university, attending courses and returning home at night, he will have to move to another city to study certain disciplines. That will restrict access, but worse than that, it will change the nature of universities. It will change the nature of what was once and for a thousand years held as the ideal, that university is a place in which people develop a kind of wholeness, a kind of universality. In fact, once it was not called "a" university but "the" university. It was part of the universe of knowledge.
However, the Government is promoting, by redirecting money away from universities and established colleges into short-term and narrow training projects, the destruction of any sense of universality in education. It is directing people to narrow training which will lock them into certain occupations. Also the Government is encouraging a situation in which the faculties of universities such as the University of Toronto are aging. They are simply not able to hire younger faculty members who have acquired the more recent and up to date techniques of any discipline, whether it is in the natural sciences, the social sciences or the arts. This means that the faculty is doomed to become less and less relevant to the present needs of the country.
The Government is also causing certain teams to be eroded or even dismantled. Certain universities will be closed. Other universities will have to cut programs or even cut departments. A team of academics built up over some years will be dispersed. A few years ago we experienced the destruction of the Avro Arrow and the destruction of a whole team of skilled people who had learned to work together in the production of what was then one of the most advanced pieces of technology in the aviation industry. Once that was destroyed, once those specialists or members of the team were dispersed, it was impossible to put them back together again, at least in Canada. We are seeing the same thing happening to our universities.
I want to refer to a few examples from the University of Toronto. In effect, that university is being penalized because it has served the country for a long time and its buildings were erected a long time ago. The physical plant of the university is not young. It is not new, some of it is not modern. At present, over $24 million of deferred maintenance is needed at the University of Toronto. Some of that is for simple repairs and some is for updating and renovation. The maintenance staff has been reduced. Some of the work is being contracted out, which does not lend itself to quality work. The buildings are deteriorating. The library is deteriorating. Since 1979 about
April 5, 1984

160 staff positions in the library have been lost. That is about one-quarter of the original staff. Yet student enrolment continues to grow. The need for books, not only by the students but by other users in the city, continues to grow. Yet the staff has been cut and hours have been cut. One of the most expensive libraries on the continent, the Robarts Library, is forced to reduce the hours at which it makes itself available to students or the public. What a waste of past money to build such an expensive library and then shut it down for parts of the week! That is what is being done through these cuts.
In Toronto there has been a great increase in the number of Spanish-speaking and Portuguese-speaking people. There is a department of Spanish and Portuguese languages, but during the last five years seven members of the faculty retired, one died, and there have been no replacements. For some of us who are of British origin that may not seem very serious. Perhaps we did not want to study Spanish or Portuguese anyway. However, I am pointing out that we have a new kind of Canada. The Portuguese people in Toronto number probably 100,000; the Spanish, probably 50,000 people. That is a considerable part of the life of that city. Those people are having their culture cut back. Their opportunity to grow in the language and literature of their forebears is being cut back as this department is cut back.
These cuts do not favour any particular country. The Italian Department is being cut back in the same way. Enrolment has doubled over the last 11 years while the number of staff has remained exactly the same. No one denies that teaching quality drops when classes are forced to enlarge, but for people of Italian heritage, the quality of university education in their heritage has now been cut in the sense that they are forced to attend classes that are twice the size. Specialists in fields such as the Renaissance, which is perhaps of greater importance to Italy than to any other country, have left the department and have not been replaced.
Slavic studies in the same way have been cut back. The department of Slavic studies serves Polish, Ukranian, Czechoslovakian, Russian and Hungarian students, that is students in those languages. Sometimes there is only one faculty person left in each of those languages. In other words, a bare minimum. If for any reason that person should leave, it is not clear that there will be a replacement.
It might be argued that Canada cannot afford the luxury of things like literature, poetry, history and so on. I would not agree with the argument, but some people may want to argue that we have to get on with the new physical sciences, the new natural sciences, the new kinds of mathematics and computer work, in fact, universities are cutting those back too. It is all the more remarkable that they should be cutting back on computer science, industrial engineering, general mathematics, engineering science and mechanical engineering, because the Government, like the governments of the provinces, has been making much of those needs-that we need to develop high-tech and that we need to develop engineering for megaprojects up North. They have been making much of the fact that we
will have a great boom in Canada because of the development of new technologies.
Mr. Speaker, with your leave, may I call it one o'clock and resume at three o'clock?

OLYMPIC GAMES
speechtext:

subtopic: LAY-OFFS AT SAINT JOHN, N. B.
LAY-OFFS AT SAINT JOHN, N. B.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian Pacific Railway is trimming its operations and lopping five employees off its Saint John payroll. The job losses cannot be justified because of technological improvements or a decrease in traffic, because this is not the case.

April 5, 1984
Last April I spoke before this House in defence of CP employees in Saint John. At that time I told the House that in the previous 15 months some 32 CP clerical jobs had been lost and that eight more were on the chopping block. Again, five more jobs are to be lost between now and April 15.
If I were to ask the Minister what he intends to do to protect the jobs of the Saint John railway employees, I have little doubt that he would boast about the 375,000 jobs that will be created as a result of Canada's rail expansion. This employment is indeed welcomed. However, there is little evidence to indicate that it will benefit the rail employees in Saint John, New Brunswick. The men and women in the Saint John facilities want to keep their jobs. They want to be able to do meaningful work and to support their families. They want to live with dignity. They are not impressed with the razzmatazz of rail expansion in the West. Service in the East is being cut to the bone as jobs are being terminated. I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) to turn his eyes eastward and press Canadian Pacific to stop its lay-offs. Maritime employees deserve the same employment potential as their western counterparts.

maintopic: "MAKE-A-WISH" FOUNDATION HELP FOR TERMINALLY ILL CHILDREN
"MAKE-A-WISH" FOUNDATION HELP FOR TERMINALLY ILL CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this day of the National Prayer Breakfast let me share with you and all Hon. Members an idea which originated in Phoenix, Arizona, but which could spread like wildfire here in Canada, thanks to the Ancaster Optimist Club in my riding. The non-profit "Make-a-wish" Foundation deals with terminally ill children. It seeks to transfer a little person's fantasy into an actual experience. Let me give just two of many examples.
One little girl's last wish was to help light the Christmas tree on the White House front lawn. The Foundation flew her to Washington, she helped President Reagan light the tree, and she died a few days later.
A ten-year old Phoenix boy had dreamed of being a fireman. When the "Make-a-wish" Foundation was notified, the little guy was made honorary firefighter for the day. He was wheeled around on the hook and ladder rig, and he tried out the high-pressure hose on unsuspecting customers in a supermarket parking lot. The Phoenix Fire Department became attached to the little boy. He went into a relapse and off-duty firemen erected an aerial ladder to his eighth-floor hospital room to enter through the window to visit the boy until the day he died.
I want to see the "Make-a-wish" Foundation take root in Canada. I am proud that the Ancaster Optimists are taking the lead to be first in Canada in wanting to help terminally ill kids make their fondest wishes come true. Hon. Members can get in touch with me for further information on the "Make-a-wish" Foundation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY RETIREMENT FOR PENITENTIARY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that some of my constituents are asking to have the Public Service Superannuation Act amended, adding a provision that will allow employees who work in federal penitentiaries to retire early, that is, after twenty years of service instead of twenty-five. In April 1977, a sub-committee of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs recommended the option of early retirement for such employees. The present Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and his predecessors have given the matter careful thought, but to date, the employees concerned have been unsuccessful in their efforts to have an amendment to the Public Service Superannuation Act tabled in the House. As one of my constituents said, and I quote: "Since my colleagues and I work in an environment like the one described in connection with the recent incidents at Archambault, and do so to protect the public, is it unreasonable to ask, as a special favour, to be released from that environment a little sooner, in recognition of our many years of dedicated service? The mental and physical tension is far more debilitating in penitentiaries than in most other departments. We feel we should be able to leave the service with dignity and perhaps embark on a second career or at least enjoy our retirement during the years we have left. The average age of inmates during incarceration remains constant, but we get older, and sometimes we have the impression that our sentence is worse than theirs."
Mr. Speaker, there would certainly be a case for the Solicitor General, once studies and consultations have been completed, to table a Bill to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and provide for early retirement for employees in federal penitentiaries.

APPEARANCE OF REPRESENTATIVE BEFORE SENATE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Zehdi Terzi of the PLO appeared this morning at a committee in the other place. I understand that he confirmed that the PLO remains committed to the non-recognition of Israel, and also to terrorism.
Why is today's meeting necessary? A sub-committee of the Senate met with several officials of the PLO last November in the Middle East, including the Chairman of the Palestine National Council. subtopic: CUTS IN FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CRISIS CENTRES IN MANITOBA
CUTS IN FUNDING FOR WOMEN'S CRISIS CENTRES IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during this time of high unemployment many Canadian families are feeling economic hardship and the resultant emotional and social upheaval as well. Alcoholism, family breakup, and physical abuse are all results of the frustration and depression felt by many Canadians.
Now, more than ever, Canadians need social agencies such as crisis and rehabilitation centres. Throughout Manitoba a number of women's crisis centres, including the Flin Flon Committee for Women and Children in Crisis, and the Aurora House in The Pas, have this year had their funding eliminated
or severely cut back under the Canada Works Program. Muriel Smith, the Manitoba minister responsible for community services, has offered her assistance. It is also the responsibility of the federal Government to continue funding for the social agencies that it helped to create in the first place. In our present economic conditions, the number of people needing these services is increasing.
If the Government is willing to see unemployment levels remain at the present high levels, it should also be willing to take responsibility for the consequences, for the endangered mental and physical health of victims of the recession. The federal Government must also be willing: to provide the necessary funding to help both the victims and those agencies that are willing to offer a helping hand.

COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR TAXPAYERS ACTING ON ADVICE GIVEN BY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the Minister's attention another aspect of his letter. He talks about the need for improved communications and improved training. Is the Minister prepared to propose a change in the Department's procedures, and in the future, if taxpayers act on the advice given by officials in the Department which later proves to be wrong and find themselves suffering financially as a result of this bad advice, will the Minister be prepared to offer compensation to those taxpayers to ensure that they do not suffer as a result of bad advice given by the Department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR TAXPAYERS ACTING ON ADVICE GIVEN BY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reached the conclusion long ago, Mr. Speaker, after watching the Hon. Member and listening to his questions, that I was far better equipped than he to run the Department of National Revenue. However, my innate modesty has always prevented me from saying so.
I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the basis of our system is self-assessment. According to this fundamental principle, the taxpayer is responsible for determining and declaring the full amount of tax owing and for paying those taxes. Of course, the Government, in this case the Department of National Revenue, should help taxpayers as much as possible in filing their returns, and it should provide the necessary information to help them understand fully the various provisions of the Income Tax Act.
However, the Hon. Member will understand that, because of the nature of the system, in the final instance not the Department, but the taxpayer is responsible for filing his income tax return. In the final instance, taxpayers are responsible and have a duty to file their returns and to sign them as being correct.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY
SOCIAL SECURITY
subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF UNEMPLOYED IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. There is a report out today that in the Province of British Columbia one person out of five is either collecting unemployment insurance or welfare. In fact the situation has gotten so bad that hundreds are being turned away from food banks in the City of Vancouver. When the Government has been asked about this in the past, the answer has always been either a reference to some kind of safety net program, or the issue has been dismissed as one involving another jurisdiction. Given the reality that we now have an emergency in British Columbia with people not even being able to find food to eat, what does the Government of Canada plan to do about it?

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY
subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF UNEMPLOYED IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has in good part given the answer to his own question. We have, indeed, a number of social programs which the federal Government is providing. One of them is unemployment insurance. The others are old age security payments, and support for families through child tax credits and family allowances. There is, in addition, the social assistance program for which the federal Government pays 50 per cent and which is administered by the provinces.
The Government of British Columbia is the Government administering the social assistance program. The Government of British Columbia is determining who is eligible for those programs. And the Government of British Columbia is deciding how much should be paid to these particular individuals. We are paying 50 per cent of the bill, but the criteria to which I referred are determined by the Government of British Columbia.
My friend may be unhappy with the Constitution we live under in this country. He may feel that we should change the constitutional arrangements with regard to social security and social programs. However, as long as we have a federation in this country, there are a number of programs which are under
April 5, 1984

provincial responsibility and which the federal Government participates in financing.
The cases the Hon. Member refers to particularly, whether it is in terms of food support or social assistance, are totally under provincial government responsibility. The Hon. Member knows of a number of events which have occurred arising out of decisions by that provincial Government in the last few months which have not helped the economic situation in British Columbia.

The Minister has indicated that we were ready and willing to talk with them to see whether there was the possibility of an agreement on expanded reforestation programs, but the federal Government cannot just barge in and tell the provinces to abandon their responsibilities. The federal Government cannot just move in and do what the provinces are not only entitled to do but are responsible for doing.
My friend is raising a red herring in that regard. He has the answer in his own question.

Canadians cannot take the jolt of an increase in interest rates every week. Will the Minister use his good offices to change the plan for establishing the bank rate, rather than tying it to an auction which is supposed to take place at the Bank of Canada offices every week? Will he make an interest rate that is appropriate for the growth of the country?
He can interfere with the exchange rate by using all sorts of reserves to prop up or prop down the dollar as the case may be. Why can he not use the Bank of Canada and establish a bank rate for the chartered banks to borrow from the Bank of Canada, to establish some consistency and stability in interest rates in our country?

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEW MECHANISM TO ESTABLISH BANK RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend seems to be worrying very much about an increase of three one-hundredths of one per cent today. In the United States on the same day most banks have been increasing their prime rates by .5 per cent. I would be much more concerned about the evolution of the interest rate in the United States. The change that took place in the Bank of Canada tender today was very minimal.
My friend is suggesting an alternative policy of artificially setting an interest rate in this country. The Bank of Canada rate has been set on the basis of tenders for a very long time, indeed many, many years. I suggest that if he really wants to help the situation he should come every Thursday and bid and lower the rate. Let him bid below the market and it will help bring the bid down. Otherwise, the bid is determined by the market and very much by what is happening in the United States.
I would like it to be different, but the fact is that this is the real world in which we are living, and the Hon. Member knows it.

Mr. Speaker, I should indicate that the application for a rate increase which has been made by Bell Canada is presently in front of the CRTC. I should also indicate that the Government has an over-all policy, as enunciated by the Minister of
April 5, 1984

Finance, with respect to the percentage amount of increase that could be granted during the course of the next year. The Minister of Finance has already indicated quite clearly that these increases cannot exceed the rate of 4 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude what I was saying before lunch by pointing out that the Government's lack of drive for the education of the whole person matches its lack of drive for the development of Canada as a whole. The Government's policy is to sell off Canada piece by piece-some coal to Japan, some gas to the United States, some timber to anyone who will take it, and so on. It is a piecemeal policy, a very short-ranged and short-sighted policy. It does not have in it any concept of serving the people of Canada or any concept of providing essentially for the needs of the people of Canada, including the needs of Canadians to
April 5, 1984

grow, to develop, to have jobs and to participate in the Government of the country.
This is the way the Government is treating universities through the cut this year and the one last year. The result is that there will be a decrease in the development of the independent mind and spirit, which has been the hallmark of the university. There will be more narrow training which locks people into limited occupations. There will be more limited service to the multinational corporations which are buying up our country and shipping it out. There will be damage to Canadian culture. There will be damage to Canadian industry through the loss of what the universities contribute to research and development. There will be damage to a whole generation of young people in Canada, the young people who are now told there are no jobs for them and nowhere for them to study. They will be told in a few years that they are not fit for jobs because they are not trained. They did not train because we will not have given them the means of training, let alone the means of education.
There will be damage to women who at this time for several reasons are capable of moving into the work force, are wanted in the workforce and want to be in the workforce. They will be hindered severely from getting the education they need. Worst of all, there will be damage to the morale of the country because when the Government says there is no future for our universities, that is a way of saying there is no future for Canada. Therefore, it is a sad day that this Bill has now come to third reading. It will be a sad day if the Government forces this Bill through Parliament.

I mention that date because only a few days previously, Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act, had also been in the House for second reading. In many ways there are similarities between these two Bills.
